## Transcript Storage & Git History

### Where data is stored

When you use Entire with an AI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Factory AI Droid, Copilot CLI, Pi), session transcripts, user prompts, and checkpoint metadata are committed to **your own git repository**. They stay out of your working branches' history, but they live in the same repo and travel with it.

Exactly where depends on the [checkpoint backend](architecture/ref-checkpoint-backend.md) the repo uses:

| Backend | Committed checkpoints land in | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `git-refs` (default for new repos) | One ref per checkpoint: `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>` | Not a branch. Pushed individually, and fetched individually on demand |
| `git-branch` (legacy) | Subtrees of one long-lived branch, `entire/checkpoints/v1` | A branch, so it shows up in branch listings, CI branch triggers, and platform previews |

`entire status` shows which backend a repo is on. The redaction described in this document applies identically to both — the pipeline is shared; only the destination differs. Where the distinction matters below, it is called out.

Entire also creates temporary local **shadow branches** (e.g. `entire/<commit>-<worktree>`) as working storage during a session, on both backends. Metadata written there — transcripts, prompts, incremental checkpoint data, subagent transcripts — goes through the same redaction pipeline as a committed checkpoint. **Code-file snapshots, however, are written as raw blobs of your working tree without redaction**, so any hardcoded secrets in your source code would appear unredacted on the shadow branch. Gitignored files (e.g., `.env`) are filtered out of these snapshots as a partial defense. Shadow branches are **not** pushed by Entire; do not push them manually, because unredacted source content would be visible on the remote. They are cleaned up when session data is condensed into a checkpoint at commit time.

Anyone with access to your repository can read committed checkpoint data: the full prompt/response history and session metadata. Note that transcripts capture all tool interactions — including file contents, MCP server calls, and other data exchanged during the session. Per-checkpoint refs are less *visible* than a branch, but they are not less accessible: a `git fetch` of `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` reads them just as well.

If your repository is **public**, this data is visible to the entire internet.

### What Entire redacts automatically

Entire automatically scans transcript and metadata content before writing it to a git object. Five always-on secret detection methods plus a configurable scanner layer (pattern matching, method 2 below) run during condensation, plus a conditional seventh pass for user-defined secret rules (see [Customizing redaction](#customizing-redaction) below), an opt-in eighth pass for PII (see [Optional PII redaction](#optional-pii-redaction) below), and an opt-in ninth pass that shells out to the OpenAI Privacy Filter model (see [Optional OpenAI Privacy Filter](#optional-openai-privacy-filter-opf) below):

1. **Entropy scoring** — Identifies high-entropy strings (Shannon entropy > 4.5) that look like randomly generated secrets, even if they don't match a known pattern.

Three places retain content that OPF *didn't* redact, with different lifetimes. Understanding them matters if your threat model goes beyond "what reaches the remote":

| Location | Redaction level | Lifetime | Reaches remote? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` | **None — raw** | Until the session's data is cleaned up (`entire clean`) | No |
| The agent's own transcript (e.g. `~/.claude/projects/…`) | **None — raw** | Owned and managed by the agent | No |
| Shadow branch `entire/<commit>-<worktree>` | 8-layer | Auto-deleted after the next successful push (only when its session has ended cleanly) | No |
| Unreachable git objects after pre-push rewrite | 8-layer | Until `git gc --prune` (default `gc.pruneExpire` is 2 weeks) | No |
| Reflog `git reflog show entire/checkpoints/v1` | 8-layer tips | Default `gc.reflogExpire` is 90 days | No |
| `<remote>/entire/checkpoints/v1` | 9-layer (after OPF rewrite) | Until you delete the branch on the remote | Yes |

`.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` is Entire's own local working copy of the transcript, written mode `0600`. It is *sanitized* (agent state that cannot be replayed out of a checkpoint is stripped) but **not redacted** — redaction happens on the way into a git object, not on this file. It is the input the shadow-branch walk and condensation read from.

The agent's own transcript is never modified at all. Entire reads from it and leaves it alone, because the agent is writing to it continuously and editing under the agent's feet would corrupt the session.

To aggressively scrub the unreachable git objects from the pre-push rewrite (instead of waiting for the 2-week GC window):

```fish
git reflog expire --expire-unreachable=now refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1
git gc --prune=now
```

This is I/O-heavy on large repositories; it's not run automatically. If you want it as part of your push workflow, wrap `git push` in a script that invokes it after a successful push.

Verifying it's working:

```fish
# After enabling OPF, run an agent turn that includes a name in the prompt,
# e.g. "Create notes.txt with: Alice Johnson reviewed the proposal."

| Factory AI Droid | `.factory/settings.json`      | JSON hooks config |
| Gemini CLI       | `.gemini/settings.json`       | JSON hooks config |
| OpenCode         | `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts` | TypeScript plugin |
| Pi               | `.pi/extensions/entire/index.ts` | TypeScript extension |

You can enable multiple agents at the same time — each agent's hooks are independent. Entire detects which agents are active by checking for installed hooks, not by a setting in `settings.json`.

### Checkpoint Remote

By default, checkpoint data rides along with your own pushes — but only to **one** remote, the elected checkpoint sync remote. Entire picks it in this order:

1. `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`, if set. This is fail-closed: if it names a remote that isn't configured, checkpoints don't sync.
2. A remote captured from your own habits: the first push whose target matches the branch's declared push destination elects that remote, announces it on stderr, and carries the checkpoints. The first capture sticks.
3. `origin`
4. The sole remote, if the repo has exactly one
5. The first remote in `.git/config` order

A push to any *other* remote carries no checkpoint data. `entire status` shows the current destination, where it came from, and how many checkpoints are unpushed. This matters if you push code to several remotes: checkpoints go to exactly one of them.

If instead you want checkpoint data in a separate repo (e.g., a private repo for a public project), configure `checkpoint_remote` with a structured provider and repo. A dedicated `checkpoint_remote` is addressed directly and is exempt from the single-remote election above:

```json
{
  "strategy_options": {
    "checkpoint_remote": {
      "provider": "github",
      "repo": "myorg/checkpoints-private"
    }
  }
}
```

Or via the CLI:

```bash
entire enable --checkpoint-remote github:myorg/checkpoints-private
```

Entire derives the git URL automatically using the same protocol (SSH or HTTPS) as your push remote. It will:

- Fetch the checkpoint branch locally if it exists on the remote but not locally (one-time)
- Push checkpoint data to the checkpoint repo instead of your default push remote
- Ignore the setting if it looks inherited rather than yours, and push checkpoints to your own push remote instead. `checkpoint_remote` is normally committed in `.entire/settings.json`, so cloning or forking a project inherits it — without this, a contributor's session data would be pushed into the upstream project's checkpoint repo. A setting is treated as yours when it lives in the gitignored `.entire/settings.local.json`, or when your `origin` **and every push URL** of the remote you are pushing to are owned by the same account or org as the checkpoint repo. Requiring the push destination too covers contributors who cloned the upstream repo and added their own fork, where `origin` belongs to the upstream project rather than to them; requiring every push URL covers mirror-style remotes that fan out to several repositories
- If your checkpoint repo is owned by a different account or org than `origin`, configure it in `.entire/settings.local.json` so it is always honored
- If the remote is unreachable, warn and continue without blocking your main push

#### `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN`

content.content:
#### `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN`

`ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN` allows you to provide a dedicated token for checkpoint repository operations, without modifying the credentials used for your primary repository.

When this environment variable is set, Entire behaves as follows:

- Injects the token into HTTPS Git operations used for checkpoint fetch and push
- If `checkpoint_remote` is configured:
  - Prefers an HTTPS URL for the checkpoint remote when a token is present, even if the repository’s `origin` uses SSH
- If `checkpoint_remote` is not configured:
  - Falls back to using the default `origin` remote
- If `checkpoint_remote` configuration cannot be loaded:
  - Falls back to `origin`
  - If `origin` is a valid SSH or HTTPS Git remote, Entire converts it to an HTTPS URL to enable token-based authentication

## 1. Discovery — which commits get re-redacted

**git-branch** (`/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/worktree-silver-harbor-a927/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_opf_rewrite.go`)

**git-refs** (`/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/worktree-silver-harbor-a927/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_opf_refs.go`)
- **Yes, it walks the push-discovery queue.** `checkpoint.PushQueueForRepo` `:36`, then `queue.Peek()` `:41` (deliberately Peek, not Drain — `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` owns draining). Empty queue → no-op `:45-47`. Queue entries not present locally are skipped, not pruned (`partitionLocalRefs` `:84`).
- **Per queued ref it walks first-parents back to the first commit carrying the trailer.** `unappliedAncestry` `:93`, implementation `:184-204`: loop over `c.ParentHashes[0]` (`:200`), `if trailers.HasOPFApplied(c.Message) { base = h; break }` (`:192-195`), chain reversed to ancestor-first (`:202`). **Your claim is CONFIRMED.** At a root with no trailer anywhere, `base = plumbing.ZeroHash` and the whole chain is rewritten as a fresh orphan chain.
- **"Steady state = stops at the tip's parent" is confirmed but only when exactly one new commit landed since the last OPF push.** Test `TestRewriteQueuedCheckpointRefsWithOPF_StopsAtTrailedParent` (`manual_commit_opf_rewrite_test.go:1030-1043`) asserts exactly this. But each write to a checkpoint advances the ref by one commit (`refs_store.go:203-213`, called from `writeSession`, `backfillTranscript`, `backfillSummary`, `backfillAttribution`), so a turn that creates + backfills transcript + backfills summary between pushes yields a 3-commit chain. Accurate phrasing: "stops at the first trailered ancestor — in steady state that is the last commit the previous push OPF'd, i.e. usually the tip's parent."
- Also note: already-applied ancestors are **not** re-parented on the refs path — they are the boundary and stay byte-identical (`:22-23`; test asserts `require.Equal(t, after, refHashes(...))` at `:955-957`). This differs from the v1 path, which re-parents applied commits onto the new chain (`:388-405`).

## 2. Fail-closed behavior, per backend — verified, they do differ

git-branch: every error from `RewriteUnpushedV1WithOPF` is **returned from `prePush`** (`/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/worktree-silver-harbor-a927/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_push.go:164-171`), so the hook exits non-zero and the user's `git push` aborts.

git-refs: `runOPFForCheckpointRefs` returns `false` on any failure and `prePushCheckpointRefs` does `return nil` (`manual_commit_push.go:399-401`), so **the user's push proceeds**; refs stay queued because Peek (not Drain) was used and `flushCheckpointRefsQueue` never runs. A warning goes to both the log and `stderrWriter` (`manual_commit_push.go:268-274`). Verified by `TestPrePushCheckpointRefs_OPFFailureWithholdsFlush` (`manual_commit_opf_rewrite_test.go:973-993`), which asserts `PrePushFromGitHook` returns nil, refs stay queued, and `ls-remote` shows nothing.

| Condition | Sentinel type | git-branch | git-refs |
|---|---|---|---|
| OPF runtime failure / breaker already tripped | `OPFRuntimeFailedError` (`rewrite.go:93-112`) | **push blocked** — `rewrite.go:312` (pre-check), `:384` (batch error) | withheld, push OK — `refs.go:56`, `:141` |
| Batch (prose-leaf) too large | `OPFBatchTooLargeError` (`rewrite.go:168-178`) | **push blocked** — `rewrite.go:374` | withheld — `refs.go:134` |
| Raw blob bytes too large | `OPFRawBytesTooLargeError` (`rewrite.go:228-240`) | **push blocked** — `rewrite.go:360` | withheld — `refs.go:117` |
| Zero effective categories | `OPFNoCategoriesError` (`rewrite.go:127-137`) | **push blocked** — two gates: decision gate `manual_commit_opf_prompt.go:49-53,74` → `manual_commit_push.go:145`, and rewrite gate `rewrite.go:303` | withheld — decision gate → `manual_commit_push.go:242-244`; rewrite gates `refs.go:53`, `:139` |
| Bootstrap cap exceeded | `BootstrapTooLargeError` (`rewrite.go:59-68`) | **push blocked** — `rewrite.go:292`, **only when the remote has no v1** (`if remoteTip.IsZero()`, `:290`) | withheld — `refs.go:100-102`, applied **per queued ref, on every push**, not just bootstrap |
| Divergence | `V1DivergedError` (`rewrite.go:43-52`) | **push blocked** — `rewrite.go:279` | **no equivalent check exists.** The refs half does no merge-base/divergence analysis at all (`refs.go:26-28`). Divergence is handled later, at push time, by the non-force refspec being rejected → per-ref `fetch`+cherry-pick replay (`push_common.go:72-95`), and that path is fail-*soft* (logged, ref left queued, `manual_commit_push.go:409-414`) |
| CAS conflict (local ref moved mid-rewrite) | git-branch: `V1RefMovedError` (`rewrite.go:73-82`, raised in `atomicSetV1Ref` `:813-830` on `storage.ErrReferenceHasChanged`). git-refs: **no sentinel** — plain `fmt.Errorf("update checkpoint ref %s: %w", ...)` (`refs.go:169-174`) | **push blocked** | withheld |
| User Ctrl-C / Abort at prompt | `errOPFAbortedByUser` (`manual_commit_push.go:27`) | **push blocked** — `manual_commit_push.go:148-149` | **withheld, push proceeds** — `manual_commit_push.go:246-248` |

Two extra notes:
- The refs half is atomic w.r.t. rebuilding (all commits rebuilt before any ref is touched, `refs.go:145-164`, test `:959-971`), but the CAS loop `:168-175` is **not atomic across refs**: a failure on ref *k* leaves refs 1..k-1 already rewritten. They stay queued and push (OPF-applied) on the next attempt, so it's safe but not "nothing moved".
- The checkpoint-policy gate runs *before* OPF on both paths and `return nil`s (`manual_commit_push.go:128-131` and `:390-392`), so a blocked policy skips OPF entirely on both backends without failing the push.

## 3. Ref update semantics

- git-branch: single CAS on `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` (`rewrite.go:407`, `atomicSetV1Ref` `:813-830`).
- git-refs: **yes, each ref is rewritten in place** — same ref name, new tip, CAS'd with the expected old hash (`refs.go:168-175`, `repo.Storer.CheckAndSetReference`).
- **The push is still fast-forward-only / non-force.** Refspec is `ref:ref` with no leading `+` (`push_common.go:62-66`), and the doc comment at `push_common.go:47-57` is explicit: "fast-forward-only (NOT a force push)… a non-fast-forward update is REJECTED rather than silently overwriting the remote. We deliberately do not force." Recovery retry is also non-force (`push_common.go:76-78`).
- Why the rewrite doesn't break fast-forward: the new chain is parented on `base`, which is the already-pushed trailered commit, so the new tip is still a descendant of the remote tip. Locally the ref move is *not* a fast-forward (old commits become unreachable) — same as v1.

## 4. Caps — actual values and env vars

| Cap | Default | Env var | Applies to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Un-OPF'd commit count | **100** (`bootstrapDefaultLimit`, `rewrite.go:142`) | **`ENTIRE_OPF_BOOTSTRAP_LIMIT`** (`rewrite.go:143`; `resolveBootstrapLimit` `:146-158`, accepts an int > 0 or `unlimited` → `math.MaxInt`; anything else silently falls back to 100) | **BOTH halves — but with different triggers.** v1: only when the remote has no v1 (`rewrite.go:290-294`), counted over all unpushed commits. refs: **always**, counted **per queued ref's un-trailered ancestry** (`refs.go:100-102`) |
| Cumulative prose-leaf bytes handed to OPF | **2 MiB** = `2 * 1024 * 1024` (`batchDefaultLimit`, `rewrite.go:185`) | **`ENTIRE_OPF_BATCH_LIMIT`** (`rewrite.go:186`; `resolveBatchLimit` `:189-201`, int > 0 or `unlimited`) | both (`rewrite.go:372-375`, `refs.go:132-135`). Measured by `redact.SumProseLeafBytes` (`/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/worktree-silver-harbor-a927/redact/batch.go:202-222`), a conservative over-estimate — it does not dedupe identical leaves the way the actual batch does |
| Cumulative **raw blob bytes** buffered in memory | **200 MiB** — derived, `batch limit × 100` (`rawByteCapMultiplier = 100`, `rewrite.go:247`; `scaleBatchLimit` `:207-215`, saturates at `MaxInt` so `unlimited` really is unlimited) | **no dedicated env var** — scales with `ENTIRE_OPF_BATCH_LIMIT` | both (`rewrite.go:337,359-361`; `refs.go:79,113-118`). Checked incrementally as blobs load, so it fires *before* the leaf cap on a pathological push. **The doc currently does not mention this cap or `OPFRawBytesTooLargeError` at all** |
| Per-invocation OPF timeout | **30 s** (`redact/opf.go:62-64`, applied in `ConfigurePrivacyFilter`) | settings `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.timeout_seconds` (`settings.go:329`), wired at `strategy/common.go:543-549` | both |

Scoping difference worth stating in the doc: on refs the byte caps are cumulative **across the whole flush** (all queued refs), while the commit cap is **per ref** (`refs.go:59-61` comment says exactly this).

## 5. The `Entire-OPF-Applied` trailer

- **Written by both halves**, via the shared `rebuildCheckpointCommit` → `trailers.AppendOPFAppliedTrailer` (`rewrite.go:575`; called from `rewrite.go:400` and `refs.go:157`). Key/value defined at `/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/worktree-silver-harbor-a927/cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:59,64`; only the literal `true` counts (`HasOPFApplied`, `:262-275`); appending is idempotent (`AppendOPFAppliedTrailer`, `:317-324`).
- **It is the discovery watermark only for git-refs** (`refs.go:192`). On git-branch the watermark is the remote tip; there the trailer is only a per-commit "skip re-redaction, just re-parent" flag (`rewrite.go:341`, `:555`).
- Nothing at commit time writes it — condensation is regex-only by design (`checkpoint/persistent.go:691-692`, `:2518-2520`, `checkpoint/prompts.go:27`).
- Trailer survives the divergence replay path: `cherryPickOnto` preserves the original message (`strategy/metadata_reconcile.go:421` comment, `createCherryPickCommit`).

## 6. Where un-redacted-by-OPF content persists — git-refs equivalents

- **Local per-checkpoint refs `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`** (prefix at `/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/worktree-silver-harbor-a927/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/refs_naming.go:16`): **yes — 8-layer before push, 9-layer after the rewrite.** Written 8-layer by condensation (`refs_store.go:203-213`), rewritten in place to 9-layer at pre-push (`refs.go:168-175`). These refs are **never deleted** after push — post-push cleanup only deletes shadow branches under `refs/heads/entire/...` (`strategy/cleanup.go:226-227`, `DeleteShadowBranchesIfUnchanged`), so the 9-layer content is the durable local state.
- **Unreachable objects**: same as v1 — the pre-rewrite 8-layer commits/trees/blobs become unreachable and wait for `git gc --prune`. Add `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` to the scrub recipe.
- **Reflog: effectively no concern for `refs/entire/checkpoints/*`.** Two reasons: (a) all checkpoint-ref writes go through go-git's storer (`SetReference` / `CheckAndSetReference`) and go-git does not append reflog entries on ref writes — `storage/filesystem/dotgit/dotgit.go:840 SetRef` has no reflog call, and reflog is a separate opt-in `AppendReflog` API; (b) git's own `core.logAllRefUpdates=true` default only auto-logs `refs/heads/*`, `refs/remotes/*`, `refs/notes/*` and `HEAD`, so even the reftable seam (`/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/worktree-silver-harbor-a927/cmd/entire/cli/gitrepo/reftable.go:195-238`, which shells out to `git update-ref`) does not create one for `refs/entire/*` unless the user set `logAllRefUpdates=always`. The existing "reflog holds 8-layer v1 tips" row is a git-branch-only row.
- **Push queue file: ref names only, no content.** `entire-checkpoint-push-queue.jsonl` in the git common dir; each line is `{"ref":"refs/entire/checkpoints/…"}` (`checkpoint/pushqueue.go:23-31`, `:69`, `:172`), mode `0600` (`:73`), flock-guarded, deleted when empty (`:163-169`). Nothing redactable in it.
- **Shadow branches**: unchanged and shared by both backends (`cleanupPushedShadowBranches` is called on both paths, `manual_commit_push.go:219` and `:416`), 8-layer metadata + raw code snapshots, never OPF'd.
- **Remote-side**: `<remote>` copy of `refs/entire/checkpoints/*`, 9-layer after rewrite. Note there is **no local remote-tracking copy** — the refspec is `ref:ref` (`push_common.go:64`), so nothing lands under `refs/remotes/`.
- **Two git-refs-specific 8-layer sinks the current table misses:**
  1. **A configured git-branch *mirror*.** Mirrors are write-only and explicitly "never receive ref-level mutations such as cleanup deletes or pre-push OPF re-redaction" (`/Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/worktree-silver-harbor-a927/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/fanout.go:10-17`). So the local `entire/checkpoints/v1` mirror branch retains 8-layer content indefinitely. It is not pushed by pre-push today (`manual_commit_push.go:108-109`), so it does not reach the remote — but it does have a `refs/heads/` reflog.
  2. **A leftover `entire/checkpoints/v1` from migration.** `MigrateBranchToRefs` (`checkpoint/migrate.go:48-…`) imports from the local v1 branch and never deletes it; the 8-layer branch and its reflog survive. Also, migrated refs' commits carry no OPF trailer (message is `"Import checkpoint %s (migrated from git-branch)"`, `migrate.go:135`), so the first post-migration push re-OPFs every migrated ref — 1 commit per ref keeps the per-ref bootstrap cap happy, but the cumulative 2 MiB leaf cap is the realistic trip point.
- **Transient**: `refs/entire-fetch-tmp/...` from the divergence-recovery fetch (`push_common.go:484`) holds remote content and is removed on success (`:546`). The v1 path's `refs/entire-fetch-tmp/opf-rewrite-v1` is cleaned up in a defer (`rewrite.go:427`, `:462-468`).
- One genuine residual gap for refs: the divergence replay cherry-picks local (OPF-applied) commits onto the *fetched remote tip*, keeping the local commit's trailer (`push_common.go:576-597` → `metadata_reconcile.go:399-430`). If the remote tip was pushed 8-layer by another machine, the resulting merged tree carries that 8-layer content under an OPF-applied trailer, and the next push's walk stops there. No *new* content reaches the remote (it came from there), but it will never be OPF'd.

## 7. Verification recipe for git-refs

`git log --oneline <branch>` cannot show the trailer at all (`--oneline` prints only the subject line) — so the git-branch recipe at line 325 is already broken. Working git-refs equivalents:

```fish
# list your checkpoint refs, newest first
git for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate --format='%(refname) %(objectname:short)' refs/entire/checkpoints/

# check the trailer on the newest one
git for-each-ref --count=1 --sort=-committerdate --format='%(refname)' refs/entire/checkpoints/ \
  | xargs -I{} git log -1 --format='%H%n%B' {}

# or across all of them at once — %(contents) exposes the trailer block
git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short) %(trailers:key=Entire-OPF-Applied)' refs/entire/checkpoints/

# confirm the redaction landed
entire checkpoint list
entire checkpoint explain <checkpoint-id> | grep -i 'REDACTED_PERSON'

# what is still queued (nothing queued == everything flushed)
git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints/ | wc -l
cat "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/entire-checkpoint-push-queue.jsonl"
```

For git-branch the trailer-visible form is `git log -1 --format='%H%n%B' entire/checkpoints/v1` (or `git log --format='%h %(trailers:key=Entire-OPF-Applied)' -2 entire/checkpoints/v1`), not `--oneline`.

## 8. Existing OPF-section claims that are now wrong

Blanket problem: everything from line 253 (`#### When OPF actually runs`) through line 327 is written as if git-branch is the only backend, even though lines 245-247 already correctly split the two. Specific defects:

1. **:143** "the push aborts with a configuration error" (zero categories) — git-branch only. On git-refs the checkpoint flush is withheld and the push succeeds (`manual_commit_push.go:242-248`, `:399-401`).
2. **:236** "**Ctrl-C** aborts the push entirely — `git push` exits non-zero, no refs go to the remote" — git-branch only. On git-refs `OPFAbort` routes to `warnOPFCheckpointRefsWithheld` + `return false` → `return nil` (`manual_commit_push.go:246-248`); the user's push completes, refs stay queued.
3. **:240** CI consideration, "the push will abort with `OPFRuntimeFailedError`" — git-branch only; git-refs withholds.
4. **:249** "…but the push still aborts" — git-branch only.
5. **:258** "The local v1 ref **fast-forwards** atomically to the new tip" — factually wrong for both. The rewritten chain is re-parented on the remote tip (`rewrite.go:391`), so the new tip is *not* a descendant of the old local tip; it is a CAS replacement that orphans the old commits (which is what step 3 then says). Same for refs (`refs.go:168-175`).
6. **:265** "commits already carrying the trailer get re-parented into the chain" — true for v1 (`rewrite.go:388-405`), **not** for refs, where a trailered commit is the walk boundary and is left byte-identical (`refs.go:22-23`; test at `:955-957`).
7. **:271** Diverged-remote bullet — git-branch only. **The git-refs half has no divergence pre-check whatsoever** (`refs.go:26-28`); a diverged checkpoint ref surfaces at push time as a non-fast-forward rejection handled by fetch+replay (`push_common.go:72-95`), and that failure is fail-soft, not a push abort.
8. **:272** "**Bootstrap** (remote has no `entire/checkpoints/v1` yet, e.g. first push): the cap is 100 unpushed commits" — the trigger condition is git-branch-specific. On git-refs the same 100-commit cap and same `BootstrapTooLargeError`/`ENTIRE_OPF_BOOTSTRAP_LIMIT` apply on **every** push, **per queued ref's un-trailered ancestry** (`refs.go:100-102`; test `REDACTED` at `:1047-1062`). The realistic refs trigger is "OPF enabled late" or "just migrated", not "first push". The error's own message already says this (`rewrite.go:56-58`).
9. **:288** Concurrent-push bullet — two errors. (a) The quoted string "concurrent push detected" does not exist; the actual message is `entire/checkpoints/v1 moved during OPF rewrite (expected %s, found %s); another local worktree advanced the ref mid-rewrite — re-run 'git push' (no fetch needed; the move was local)` (`rewrite.go:78-81`) — and it says re-run, *not* "Fetch and retry". (b) On git-refs a CAS conflict yields a plain wrapped error (no sentinel) and withholds the flush without aborting the push (`refs.go:169-174`).
10. **:292** "Three places retain content" — the table has six rows.
11. **:300** Reflog row is git-branch-only; `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` gets no reflog under git defaults (see §6). The scrub recipe at :311-314 also only names `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1`.
12. **:305 / :309** table rows `<remote>/entire/checkpoints/v1` and the "unreachable objects" row need `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` equivalents; the mirror-branch and post-migration-leftover 8-layer sinks (§6) are missing entirely.
13. **:324** The quoted progress string `→ OpenAI Privacy Filter: scanning N checkpoints (~30s)…` does not exist in the codebase. Real strings: `→ OpenAI Privacy Filter: scanning checkpoints before push (may take ~30s)…` (non-TTY only, `manual_commit_opf_prompt.go:101`), `→ OpenAI Privacy Filter: scanning checkpoints…` (`redact/batch.go:243`), and `✓ OpenAI Privacy Filter: done (%.1fs, %d blobs)` (`redact/batch.go:249-250`). Line 229's quote is the second of these and is correct.
14. **:325 and :346** `git log --oneline … | head -2` cannot show a trailer (see §7).
15. **Missing cap**: `OPFRawBytesTooLargeError` / the 200 MiB derived raw-byte ceiling (`rewrite.go:217-247`) is undocumented on both backends. It is the cap most likely to fire first on a big push, and it has no env var of its own.
16. **:245** git-branch bullet quotes `OPF runtime failed; aborting push`. Actual text is `OPF runtime failed during pre-push rewrite (command=%q); aborting push so regex-only content isn't tagged as OPF-applied…` (`rewrite.go:99-103`).
17. **:247** git-refs bullet is accurate as written — including "a warning names the failure and states that checkpoint refs stayed queued" (`manual_commit_push.go:272-273`). Keep it.
18. **:250** Cost note's "v1 commits on git-branch, every unpushed commit on every queued ref on git-refs — into a single inference pass" is accurate: one `BatchBytesWithPrivacyFilter` call per flush across all refs (`refs.go:136`; test asserts `fake.batchCallCount() == 1` at `:942`).</result>

configuration and still works from the shared project file.

The interactive prompt offers three options and reacts to **Ctrl-C** for cancellation:

```
Run OpenAI Privacy Filter on these checkpoints?
Adds ~30s but redacts names/PII the regex layers can't catch.
Ctrl-C to cancel the push.

  ▸ Yes — run OPF this push
    No — skip OPF, push as-is
    Always — run OPF on every push from now on
```

- **Yes** runs OPF for this push only.
- **No** skips OPF for this push only; the 8-layer-redacted content reaches the remote.
- **Always** runs OPF this push AND writes `prompt_default: "always"` to `.entire/settings.local.json` so future pushes don't ask.
- **Ctrl-C** aborts the push entirely — `git push` exits non-zero, no refs go to the remote.

Non-interactive contexts (CI, scripted pipes with no TTY) skip the prompt and run OPF automatically when enabled, printing `→ OpenAI Privacy Filter: scanning checkpoints…` to stderr so the wait isn't silent. Set `ENTIRE_OPF=no` to skip OPF in those contexts without disabling the feature globally.

**CI consideration**: if you've enabled OPF locally and your CI runs `git push` (e.g. an agent-driven workflow), the CI push will attempt to run OPF too. If the `opf` binary isn't installed in CI, the push will abort with `OPFRuntimeFailedError` rather than silently shipping under-redacted content — by design, since "I enabled OPF" should mean "no content leaves my machines without OPF." The remedies are (a) install `opf` in CI, (b) set `ENTIRE_OPF=no` for CI pushes, or (c) set `prompt_default: "never"` if you only want OPF on interactive pushes.

OPF failures at push time are **fail-closed**: if OPF is not on PATH, fails to start, or times out during the pre-push rewrite, the per-process circuit breaker trips and no under-redacted content reaches the remote. The intent is that "the user enabled OPF" means "I do not want unredacted content leaving this machine" — falling back to 8-layer silently on the push path would violate that contract. Fix the install or set `ENTIRE_OPF=no` for a one-off push.

How that is enforced depends on the checkpoint backend, because they have different escape hatches:

- **git-branch**: the rewrite aborts the push with `OPF runtime failed; aborting push`. Your `git push` exits non-zero. The checkpoint branch travels with that push, so refusing the push is the only way to withhold it.
- **git-refs**: checkpoint refs are pushed separately from your branch and stay queued when they are not flushed, so the failure withholds the checkpoint push and lets your own `git push` succeed. Nothing under-redacted ships either way. This is not silent: a warning names the failure and states that checkpoint refs stayed queued for the next push.

(The circuit breaker is per-process, so a broken install costs one warning instead of one timeout per blob — but the push still aborts.)

Cost note: each shell-out loads the OPF model (~1.5B parameters on CPU). The pre-push rewrite batches **every redactable leaf across every unpushed commit** — v1 commits on git-branch, every unpushed commit on every queued ref on git-refs — into a single inference pass, so a typical real-world push pays the model-load cost once (~6s) plus inference (~5s per 100KB of leaf content) — not multiplied by the number of commits or blobs. A 3-commit push with ~250KB of total prose content runs in ~12–15s, not the ~50–100s a per-blob flow would take. Per-commit latency is unaffected because OPF doesn't run at commit time.

#### When OPF actually runs

OPF execution lives in the pre-push hook. The flow:

1. **Post-commit** writes the checkpoint with **8-layer-only** redaction to your local `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. Fast, predictable, no OPF cost on the hot path.
2. **Pre-push** (`git push`): if OPF is enabled, the hook re-reads each unpushed `entire/checkpoints/v1` commit, runs the OpenAI Privacy Filter over its blobs to add the categories the regex layers don't catch (person names, addresses, etc.), and builds **new commits** carrying an `Entire-OPF-Applied: true` trailer. The local v1 ref fast-forwards atomically to the new tip, and the (now 9-layer-redacted) commits are what get pushed.
3. The original 8-layer-only commits become **unreachable** in the local git object database and eventually get swept by `git gc`.

p = pathlib.Path("docs/security-and-privacy.md"); s = p.read_text(); orig = s

start = s.index("#### Force-pushed remote, bootstrap, and concurrent pushes")
end = s.index("#### Persistence of un-redacted-by-OPF content")

new = """#### Divergence, caps, and concurrent pushes

The rewrite refuses to proceed in a divergent or oversized state rather than silently rebasing or shipping unscanned content. As always, `git-branch` enforces this by aborting your push and `git-refs` by withholding the checkpoint refs.

**Divergence.** On `git-branch`, if local `entire/checkpoints/v1` has commits that aren't ancestors of the remote's v1, the hook exits with a `entire/checkpoints/v1 has diverged from remote` error. Fetch the remote and either reset local v1 to the remote tip or resolve manually before pushing.

`git-refs` has no divergence pre-check, and doesn't need one: each checkpoint is its own ref, so divergence shows up at push time as a non-fast-forward rejection for that one ref. Recovery fetches the remote ref and replays the local-only commits on top, then retries — still without forcing, so the remote commit is preserved as an ancestor. A ref that can't be replayed stays queued.

**Un-OPF'd commit cap: `100` by default.** Override per push:

```fish
set -x ENTIRE_OPF_BOOTSTRAP_LIMIT 500; git push
# or fully unbounded:
set -x ENTIRE_OPF_BOOTSTRAP_LIMIT unlimited; git push
```

The two backends trip this differently. On `git-branch` it applies **only on bootstrap** — the first push, when the remote has no v1 yet — counted across all unpushed commits. On `git-refs` it applies on **every** push, counted **per queued ref** over that ref's un-trailered ancestry. In practice the `git-refs` trigger is "OPF was enabled late" or "checkpoints were just migrated from the branch", not "first push".

**Batch cap: `2 MiB` of cumulative prose-leaf content by default** (≈110s of inference), on both backends. An `OPF would run inference on …` error means you've hit it:

```fish
set -x ENTIRE_OPF_BATCH_LIMIT 10485760; git push   # 10 MiB
# or fully unbounded:
set -x ENTIRE_OPF_BATCH_LIMIT unlimited; git push
```

**Raw-byte cap: `200 MiB` of blob content buffered in memory**, on both backends. It has no env var of its own — it is derived as 100× the batch cap, so raising `ENTIRE_OPF_BATCH_LIMIT` raises it too. It is checked incrementally as blobs load, so on a pathological push (one commit carrying a huge pasted transcript) this is the cap that fires first.

The three caps protect different failure modes: the commit cap stops "100 throwaway commits", the batch cap stops "one commit with 50 MB of prose", and the raw-byte cap stops the loader exhausting memory before either of the others can be evaluated. On `git-refs` the two byte caps are cumulative across the whole flush (all queued refs together) while the commit cap is per ref.

**Concurrent push** from another worktree: both backends compare-and-swap the local ref. If another process moved it while OPF was running, `git-branch` exits with `entire/checkpoints/v1 moved during OPF rewrite …; re-run 'git push' (no fetch needed; the move was local)` and aborts. On `git-refs` the affected ref simply stays queued and the next push picks it up. Note that the `git-refs` rewrite rebuilds every commit before touching any ref, but the ref updates themselves are not atomic *across* refs: a conflict partway through leaves the earlier refs already rewritten. They stay queued and push OPF-applied next time, so this is safe — just not "nothing moved".

new = """#### Persistence of un-redacted-by-OPF content

Several places retain content that OPF *didn't* redact, with different lifetimes. Understanding them matters if your threat model goes beyond "what reaches the remote":

| Location | Redaction level | Lifetime | Reaches remote? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` | **None — raw** | Until the session's data is cleaned up (`entire clean`) | No |
| The agent's own transcript (e.g. `~/.claude/projects/…`) | **None — raw** | Owned and managed by the agent | No |
| Shadow branch `entire/<commit>-<worktree>` | 8-layer | Auto-deleted after the next successful push (only when its session has ended cleanly) | No |
| Unreachable git objects after the pre-push rewrite | 8-layer | Until `git gc --prune` (default `gc.pruneExpire` is 2 weeks) | No |
| Local `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` (`git-refs`) | 8-layer before push, 9-layer after the rewrite | Kept indefinitely — these refs are never deleted after pushing | Yes, once pushed |
| Local `entire/checkpoints/v1` (`git-branch`) | 8-layer before push, 9-layer after the rewrite | Until you delete the branch | Yes, once pushed |
| Reflog of `entire/checkpoints/v1` (`git-branch` only) | 8-layer tips | Default `gc.reflogExpire` is 90 days | No |
| A configured `git-branch` **mirror** | 8-layer, indefinitely | Until you delete the branch | No — mirrors aren't pushed at pre-push |
| A leftover `entire/checkpoints/v1` after migrating to `git-refs` | 8-layer | Until you delete the branch | No |
| The remote's copy of the pushed refs/branch | 9-layer (after OPF rewrite) | Until you delete them on the remote | Yes |

Two notes on the `git-refs` rows:

- **There is no reflog concern for `refs/entire/checkpoints/*`.** Git's `core.logAllRefUpdates` default only auto-logs `refs/heads/*`, `refs/remotes/*`, `refs/notes/*`, and `HEAD`, and Entire's checkpoint-ref writes don't append reflog entries themselves. The reflog row above is genuinely branch-only (unless you've set `logAllRefUpdates=always`).
- **The push queue holds no content.** `entire-checkpoint-push-queue.jsonl` in the git common dir stores one ref *name* per line, mode `0600`. Nothing in it is redactable.

Two `git-branch`-shaped leftovers are easy to miss once a repo has moved on:

- **A `git-branch` mirror never gets OPF'd.** Mirrors receive best-effort write fan-out only and never ref-level mutations, so a mirror branch keeps 8-layer content indefinitely. It isn't pushed at pre-push, so it doesn't reach the remote — but it is local content, and it has a `refs/heads/` reflog.
- **Migration doesn't delete the old branch.** `entire doctor migrate-checkpoints` imports from `entire/checkpoints/v1` and leaves it in place, 8-layer, along with its reflog. Migrated refs also carry no OPF trailer, so the first push after a migration re-OPFs every migrated ref — one commit per ref keeps the commit cap happy, but the 2 MiB batch cap is the realistic trip point.

`.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` is Entire's own local working copy of the transcript, written mode `0600`. It is *sanitized* (agent state that cannot be replayed out of a checkpoint is stripped) but **not redacted** — redaction happens on the way into a git object, not on this file. It is the input the shadow-branch walk and condensation read from.

The agent's own transcript is never modified at all. Entire reads from it and leaves it alone, because the agent is writing to it continuously and editing under the agent's feet would corrupt the session.

To aggressively scrub the unreachable git objects from the pre-push rewrite (instead of waiting for the 2-week GC window):

```fish
# git-refs
git reflog expire --expire-unreachable=now --all
git gc --prune=now

# git-branch
git reflog expire --expire-unreachable=now refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1
git gc --prune=now
```

This is I/O-heavy on large repositories; it's not run automatically. If you want it as part of your push workflow, wrap `git push` in a script that invokes it after a successful push.

#### Verifying OPF is working

After enabling OPF, run an agent turn whose prompt contains a name — e.g. *"Create notes.txt with: Alice Johnson reviewed the proposal."* — then commit (which stays on the fast 8-layer pipeline) and push, which is when OPF runs.

```fish
git commit -m "demo"
git push   # → "OpenAI Privacy Filter: scanning checkpoints…"
```

Then confirm the redaction landed and the trailer is present. Note that `git log --oneline` **cannot** show a trailer — it prints only the subject line — so use a format that includes the body:

```fish
# git-refs: which checkpoint refs exist, and which are OPF-applied
git for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate \\
  --format='%(refname:short)  %(trailers:key=Entire-OPF-Applied)' refs/entire/checkpoints/

# git-branch: the trailer on the latest v1 commit
git log -1 --format='%H%n%B' entire/checkpoints/v1

# either backend: confirm the content itself was redacted
entire checkpoint list
entire checkpoint explain <checkpoint-id> | grep -i 'REDACTED_PERSON'
```

If `[REDACTED_PERSON]` appears in the prompt or transcript section and the checkpoint's commit carries `Entire-OPF-Applied: true`, OPF is active.

On `git-refs` you can also confirm nothing was withheld — an absent or empty queue file means everything flushed:

```fish
cat "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/entire-checkpoint-push-queue.jsonl"
```

"""

content.content:
#### When OPF actually runs

OPF execution lives in the pre-push hook. The flow:

1. **Post-commit** writes the checkpoint with **8-layer-only** redaction to local git objects — per-checkpoint refs on `git-refs`, the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch on `git-branch`. Fast, predictable, no OPF cost on the hot path.
2. **Pre-push** (`git push`): if OPF is enabled, the hook re-reads each not-yet-OPF'd commit, runs the OpenAI Privacy Filter over its blobs to add the categories the regex layers don't catch (person names, addresses, etc.), and builds **new commits** carrying an `Entire-OPF-Applied: true` trailer. Each backend then points its own local ref at the new tip with a compare-and-swap, and the (now 9-layer-redacted) commits are what get pushed.
3. The original 8-layer-only commits become **unreachable** in the local git object database and eventually get swept by `git gc`.

The two backends differ in **how they find the commits to rewrite**:

| | `git-refs` | `git-branch` |
|---|---|---|
| What it walks | Every ref in the push-discovery queue | The `entire/checkpoints/v1` commit chain |
| Where it stops | The first ancestor already carrying `Entire-OPF-Applied: true` — the trailer is the watermark | The remote's v1 tip, fetched live (not a stale tracking ref) |
| Already-OPF'd commits | Left byte-identical; they *are* the boundary | Re-parented onto the new chain, but not re-redacted |
| Ref update | Each queued ref rewritten in place, CAS'd individually | One CAS on the local v1 ref |

In steady state the `git-refs` walk stops at the last commit the previous push OPF'd. That is usually the tip's parent, but not always: each write to a checkpoint advances its ref by one commit, so a turn that creates a checkpoint and then backfills its transcript and summary leaves a three-commit chain to rewrite.

Note that the local ref move is **not** a fast-forward on either backend — the rewritten chain replaces the old commits rather than descending from them, which is exactly why step 3 leaves them unreachable. The *push* is still fast-forward-only and never forced, because the new chain is parented on a commit the remote already has.

This means:

- **The remote only ever sees 9-layer-redacted content** when OPF is enabled.
- **Local-only commits are 8-layer-redacted** until the moment you push. If you never push, OPF never runs.
- **Re-running pre-push is idempotent** — commits already carrying the trailer are never re-redacted.

#### Divergence, caps, and concurrent pushes

The rewrite refuses to proceed in a divergent or oversized state rather than silently rebasing or shipping unscanned content. As always, `git-branch` enforces this by aborting your push and `git-refs` by withholding the checkpoint refs.

content.text:
Both files validate clean. Done with `docs/security-and-privacy.md`.

## README additions

Left the external-agent mechanism out as you asked. Added a **Vercel Projects** section plus a `vercel` config row. Verifying it turned up something worth knowing: it's a **git-branch-only** feature. The `vercel.json` merge happens in `persistent.go` (the git-branch store) and `createOrphanMetadataRef`; `refs_store.go` never touches it. Under git-refs the setting has no effect, because `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` aren't branches so Vercel never sees them. The detection doesn't check the backend, though, so you may still be prompted on a git-refs repo — I documented that rather than leaving people to wonder.

## security-and-privacy.md

**"Where data is stored"** now leads with a backend table (git-refs first) instead of asserting the v1 branch. Added the point that per-checkpoint refs are *less visible* than a branch but not less accessible — a `git fetch` of `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` reads them just as well.

**The OPF section was the real gap** — everything from "When OPF actually runs" onward was written as if git-branch were the only backend, even though two bullets above it already split the two. Fixed with a comparison table for discovery (queue-walk with the trailer as watermark vs. remote-tip boundary), and threaded the fail-closed asymmetry through every place it applies: Ctrl-C, the CI note, and zero-categories each behave differently per backend.

Things that were **wrong**, now corrected:
- **"The local v1 ref fast-forwards atomically to the new tip"** — false on both backends. The rewritten chain replaces the old commits rather than descending from them, which is precisely why the next sentence says they become unreachable. The *push* is fast-forward-only; the local move isn't.
- **"commits already carrying the trailer get re-parented"** — true for git-branch, false for git-refs, where a trailered commit *is* the boundary and stays byte-identical.
- **Bootstrap cap framing** — on git-refs the 100-commit cap applies on *every* push, per queued ref, not just on a first push. The realistic trigger is "OPF enabled late" or "just migrated", not bootstrap.
- **Divergence** — git-refs has no pre-check at all; divergence surfaces at push time as a non-fast-forward rejection with fetch-and-replay recovery.
- **Two quoted strings didn't exist in the codebase** (the concurrent-push message and a progress line), and the concurrent-push remedy said "fetch and retry" when the real message says re-run without fetching.
- **`git log --oneline | head -2` cannot show a trailer** — `--oneline` prints only the subject. That recipe was broken for git-branch too. Replaced with `%(trailers:key=…)` and `--format='%H%n%B'` forms, both of which I ran against real refs to confirm they print what I claim.
- **The 200 MiB raw-byte cap was undocumented** on both backends — and it's the one most likely to fire first on a large push, with no env var of its own.
- **"Three places retain content"** above a six-row table; the table also missed the git-refs rows, and I added two easy-to-miss 8-layer sinks: a git-branch **mirror** never gets OPF'd, and `doctor migrate-checkpoints` leaves the old branch in place.
- The raw-transcript row said `.entire/<session>.jsonl` "owned by the agent". It's `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl`, written by *Entire* — sanitized but not redacted.

One correction to something I told you earlier: I'd written that `entire status` shows the backend. It doesn't — not in text, `--detailed`, or `--json`. The doc now points at `checkpoints.primary.type` in settings. The sync-remote claim I made in the README does hold; I confirmed the destination line, the source annotation, and the unpushed counter in `status.go`.

**Left alone deliberately:** the scanner-engine, PII, rule-pack, telemetry, and vulnerability sections — all backend-agnostic and accurate as written.

# in nightly (prerelease) builds. .Prerelease is empty for a stable tag
      # (vX.Y.Z) and non-empty for a nightly tag (vX.Y.Z-nightly.*). Local
      # builds carry no stamp and use the package default ("true" = visible).
      - -X github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/experimental.Visible={{ if .Prerelease }}true{{ else }}false{{ end }}

  # git-remote-entire is the git remote helper for entire:// URLs (see
  # cmd/git-remote-entire). A small, dedicated binary shipped alongside
  # entire so `git clone entire://…` resolves it on PATH — no telemetry,
  # only the versioninfo stamp it needs for its git agent string.
  - id: git-remote-entire
    main: ./cmd/git-remote-entire
    binary: git-remote-entire
    env:
      - CGO_ENABLED=0
    goos:
      - darwin
      - linux
      - windows
    goarch:
      - amd64
      - arm64
    ldflags:

      - -X github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/versioninfo.Commit={{.ShortCommit}}

    # defaults the id filter to the project name ("cli"), which matched the

    - enabled: '{{ isEnvSet "MACOS_SIGN_P12" }}'

        - git-remote-entire

        certificate: "{{.Env.MACOS_SIGN_P12}}"

content.text:
Yes — and it's a clean win, so I've made that change and pushed it to the PR.

`./cmd/git-remote-entire` is its own `main` package, so `go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/git-remote-entire@latest` works. I checked the two things that could have made it a hollow suggestion:

- **The binary name.** Git finds a remote helper by name on `$PATH`, and `go install` names the binary after its directory — `git-remote-entire`. Exactly right, no renaming or config needed.
- **The missing ldflags.** GoReleaser only adds `-s -w` plus `versioninfo.Version`/`Commit` stamps. But `versioninfo.Load()` recovers the version from Go's module build info when ldflags left it at the default, so a `go install ...@latest` build reports its real version in the git agent string. Nothing degrades.

I also built it locally to confirm the module path resolves.

The section now installs both, with a note that you can skip the helper if you never clone over `entire://`. I dropped the old advice, which told `go install` users to switch to Homebrew/Scoop for `entire://` support — that was unnecessary.

While verifying, one genuine difference from a stable release did turn up, so I documented it: `go install` passes no ldflags, so `experimental.Visible` keeps its package default of `"true"`. A `go-install`ed `entire help` shows the experimental commands that a stable release hides. Worth saying, since it explains why someone's help output won't match a colleague's.

PR **#2216** now has two commits and stays in draft. Lint passes.

content.text:
That PR would be a no-op — the enable flow already doesn't offer the choice. I checked all three ways it could:

- **No prompt exists.** The only `huh.NewSelect` in `setup.go` is shell completion (`setup.go:2225`). There is no backend form anywhere in the tree.
- **Both first-run paths write refs silently.** `resolveFirstRunCheckpointBackend` (`setup.go:1417`) returns `firstRunCheckpointBackendDefault()` → `"refs"` with no interaction, and the non-interactive `--agent` path does the same at `setup.go:1999`. Its own comment says a storage-topology question is unanswerable during first-time setup.
- **`branch` is already explicit-only.** The single way to get it is typing `--checkpoint-backend branch`.

So what you're describing is the shipped behavior. I verified it end-to-end earlier too: a fresh `entire enable --agent claude-code` writes `{"checkpoints":{"primary":{"type":"git-refs"}}}` and nothing asks.

What's left is two bits of residue that make it *read* as if the choice were still offered — probably why it felt unfinished:

**1. A stale sentence in the architecture doc.** `docs/architecture/ref-checkpoint-backend.md:180` says new setups get "`git-refs` as the recommended pick unless the setup question chose branch." There is no setup question. That line is describing a design that didn't ship.

**2. The flag help presents them as co-equal.** On both `enable` and `configure` (`setup.go:778` and `:936`):

> `Checkpoint storage backend: refs (one git ref per checkpoint; recommended) or branch (shared entire/checkpoints/v1 branch)`

"refs … or branch" reads like a live choice with a nudge. If the intent is that branch is a legacy escape hatch, that should say so — something like `refs (default; one git ref per checkpoint) or branch (legacy shared entire/checkpoints/v1 branch)`.

My recommendation: fix the doc line, reword the flag help, and skip anything structural. Specifically **don't** hide `--checkpoint-backend` on `enable` — someone onboarding a repo that must interoperate with older clients needs it discoverable at setup time, not after the fact via `configure`.

content.content:
### Checkpoints

A **checkpoint** is a snapshot within a session—a "save point" in your work.

Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit, and the commit carries an `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailer linking the two.

**Checkpoint IDs** are 26-character ULIDs (e.g. `REDACTED`), which sort by creation time. Checkpoints written by older versions of Entire carry a legacy 12-character hex ID (e.g. `a3b2c4d5e6f7`); both formats stay readable in the same repo, and you can pass either to any command that takes a checkpoint ID.

### Checkpoint Storage

Checkpoints live in your repository's own git object store, never in your branch's history. Each checkpoint is its own git ref:

```
refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>
```

The ref points at a commit whose tree *is* that checkpoint — `metadata.json`, the per-session transcript files, and any subagent task records. `<shard>` is the last two characters of the ID, which keeps the refs evenly distributed.

Because checkpoints are independent refs, they are written, pushed, and fetched independently. There is no shared branch tip for concurrent sessions to contend on, and a reader can fetch exactly the one checkpoint it needs instead of a whole history. A checkpoint written on another machine is fetched on demand the first time you read it.

`entire enable` sets this up; there is nothing to configure. It is recorded in `.entire/settings.json` as:

```json
{
  "checkpoints": {
    "primary": { "type": "git-refs" }
  }
}
```

Inspect what a repo has locally with plain git, or through Entire:

```bash
git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints    # the raw refs
entire checkpoint list                      # checkpoints on this branch
entire checkpoint explain <id>              # one checkpoint in full
```

### How It Works

content.content:
### `entire configure`

Use `entire configure` to update non-agent settings on a repo that's already set up. Agent installation lives under `entire agent`.

Typical uses:

- Toggle telemetry
- Reinstall the Entire git hook (`--force`, `--absolute-git-hook-path`)
- Update strategy options such as `--checkpoint-remote` or `--skip-push-sessions`
- Pick the provider, model, and timeout for `entire checkpoint explain --generate` (`--summarize-provider`, `--summarize-model`, `--summarize-timeout-seconds`)

**Examples:**

```bash
# Show help and the hint pointing to 'entire agent'
entire configure

# Opt out of telemetry
entire configure --telemetry=false

# Reinstall the Entire git hook with an absolute binary path
entire configure --absolute-git-hook-path

# Update strategy options on an existing repo
entire configure --checkpoint-remote github:myorg/checkpoints-private

# Choose who generates summaries
entire configure --summarize-provider claude-code
```

Adding or removing an agent lives under `entire agent`:

```bash
entire agent add claude-code
entire agent remove claude-code
```

## Plugins

Done and pushed to #2216. The README now has **zero** mentions of the branch backend — I grepped for `git-branch`, `checkpoints/v1`, and `checkpoint-backend` and all come back empty.

**Checkpoint Storage** is now purely about refs: the layout, what the shard is, why independent refs matter (no shared tip, per-checkpoint fetch), on-demand fetch for checkpoints written elsewhere, the settings block `entire enable` writes, and three commands to inspect them.

**The format line stayed**, phrased as current vs. legacy rather than by backend: ULIDs are current, older Entire versions wrote 12-char hex, both remain readable and either can be passed to any command taking an ID.

Also removed, since they only existed to select the other backend: the `--checkpoint-backend` row from the enable flag table, its bullet and example from `entire configure`, and `git-branch` as a value in the settings table.

**One thing I cut that you asked for last turn, so flagging it explicitly: the Vercel Projects section and its `vercel` settings row are gone.** That setting only does something on the branch backend — the `vercel.json` merge lives in the git-branch store, and per-checkpoint refs aren't branches so Vercel never has anything to deploy. Documenting it meant reintroducing the backend everything else in that commit removes, in order to explain a setting that's inert on the documented path. If you'd rather keep it, say so and I'll restore it — it's one paragraph, and the commit message records why it went.

Two things worth deciding separately, both outside this PR:

**The README now diverges from what most repos actually do.** The config-less runtime fallback is still `git-branch`, so every repo set up before the refs default is on the branch backend and the README no longer describes their storage. That's fine if the README is meant to point at where things are going, but it does mean a user on an older repo won't find their `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch explained anywhere user-facing. `docs/architecture/ref-checkpoint-backend.md` covers it, and `docs/security-and-privacy.md` still documents both — which I think is right, since redaction differences are a security matter, not a "what's recommended" one.

**The flag help still presents them as co-equal** — `refs (one git ref per checkpoint; recommended) or branch (shared entire/checkpoints/v1 branch)` at `setup.go:778` and `:936`. And `docs/architecture/ref-checkpoint-backend.md:180` still refers to a "setup question" that was never built. Those are the two remaining places implying a choice exists. Want me to take them in a small follow-up?

lastPrompt: I want the README to not mention the branch backend at all then. I mean keep the line for checkpoint format (current and legacy) but the checkpoint storage section should only be about refs
